DEAR CLAUDE,--I suppose the time of year and the open window have made me want to write more than usual. What you ask, though it is easy to see, is not easy to say. I was tired with it, and I had just been reading your letter when I went to bed. So much for what I have done since I wrote last. I wonder what you will say.

You ask for my window, and my writing-table, and the things I saw as I dressed. You will see them when you come to visit me. That will not be for a long time. I cannot answer your questions about them, though I shall think about them. They may turn up in my mind for a little while some day. But I think I could answer questions about you without doing that. I think it would be a little different.

You are a thing, because you have no shape. But a thing must live somewhere; and I do not think you can live in your book. It is a person who lives in the words, who makes the words, and who can feel what they are saying and stop their saying it. You are not that person, but a thing. You are in the words, but not a part of them. They would go on, all the same, if you were taken away, but they would not keep going on by themselves. You have never done that to the words you speak to me. _September 9th._--The house is very full. The party was to have been much larger, but my aunt has been taken ill, and some of her guests have stayed at home. She has gone to a nursing home, and my aunt's niece, her only daughter, is here instead.

When I get my letters I find a telegram, sent by my aunt's doctor, saying that my aunt has had an attack of influenza, and that it is not expected that she will be able to come back to us before November.

_A Letter from the Sea._

Dear friend,

In a little while now we shall be out of the darkness into the sunshine again, and I shall see you. I am not coming home with you in the boat. I should have liked to do that, for I know where to look for you, and I should have liked to watch the sea change again into the blue and white. But I am to take a ship out with me.

I have been away with the ship for some days, and I have not seen her. But the sun is so bright and the wind so fresh that I feel as if I had only been away for a little while.

I have been thinking of you a good deal in the last two days, and wishing that you could have been with me on the ship, for we have had a new kind of sailing and a new kind of sea.
